exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Correlation Coefficient Given Variances and Covariance

question.text: The variances of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ are $5$ and $20$, respectively. Given that $\textrm{Cov}(X,Y) = 8,$ find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$
question.explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

In our case, we have

\begin{align*} \textrm {SD}[X] &= \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[X]} = \sqrt{5}, \\[3pt] \textrm {SD}[X] &= \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[Y]} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}. \end{align*}

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[X]} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{5} \cdot 2\sqrt{5}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4}{5}. \end{align*}

question.text:
$f(x,y)$ $Y=-1$ $Y=1$ $f_X$
$X=0$ $0.01$ $0.45$ $0.46$
$X=2$ $0.52$ $0.02$ $0.54$
$f_Y$ $0.53$ $0.47$ $1$

The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that \[ \textrm {E}[X]=1.08,\qquad \textrm {E}[Y]=-0.06, \qquad \textrm {SD}[X] \approx 0.9968, \qquad \textrm {SD}[Y] \approx 0.9982, \] find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

\begin{align} \textrm{E}[XY] &= \sum\limits_{x \in S_X} \sum\limits_{y \in S_Y} x y \, f(x,y) \\[5pt] &= 0\cdot (-1)\cdot 0.01 + 0\cdot 1\cdot 0.45 \\[5pt] &\phantom{=\,} + 2\cdot (-1)\cdot 0.52 + 2\cdot 1\cdot 0.02 \\[5pt] &= -1. \end{align}

Then, we compute the covariance and get

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[5pt] &= -1 - (1.08)(-0.06) \\[3pt] &= -0.9352. \end{align}

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]} \\[5pt] &\approx \dfrac{-0.9352}{ 0.9968 \cdot 0.9982} \\[5pt] &\approx -0.94, \end{align*}

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

question.explanation:

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

\begin{align} \textrm{E}[XY] &= \sum\limits_{x \in S_X} \sum\limits_{y \in S_Y} x y \, f(x,y) \\[5pt] &= (-2)\cdot (-1)\cdot 0.1 + (-2)\cdot 0 \cdot 0.2 + (-2)\cdot 1\cdot 0.2 \\[5pt] &\phantom{=\,} + 2\cdot (-1)\cdot 0.1 + 2\cdot 0 \cdot 0 + 2\cdot 1\cdot 0.4 \\[5pt] &= 0.4. \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Continuous Random Variables

question.text:
\[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} 4x^2y+\dfrac{1}{3}, & \quad {0 \leq x \leq 1, \, 0 \leq y \leq 1} \\[5pt] 0,& \quad \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that \[ \textrm {E}[X]= \dfrac{2}{3},\qquad \textrm {E}[Y]= \dfrac{11}{18}, \qquad \textrm {SD}[X]\approx 0.2582, \qquad \textrm {SD}[Y]\approx 0.2664, \] find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

\[\begin{align} \textrm E [XY] &=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} xy \, f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^1 \left[ \int_0^1 xy \cdot \left(4x^2y+\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\: \textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^1 \left[ \int_0^1 \left(4x^3y^2 + \dfrac13 xy\right) \: \textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^1 \left[x^4y^2+\dfrac16x^2y\right]_{x=0}^{x=1} \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^1 \left(y^2+\dfrac16y\right) \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\left[ \dfrac{1}{3}y^3+\dfrac1{12} y^2 \right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac1{12}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{12}. \end{align}\]

Then, we compute the covariance and get

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{12} - \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)\left(\dfrac{11}{18}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{108}. \end{align}

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]} \\[5pt] &\approx \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{1}{108}\right)}{(0.2582) \cdot (0.2664)} \\[5pt] &\approx 0.13, \end{align*}

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

question.text:
\[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{x+y}{3}, & \quad {0 \leq x \leq 2, \, 0 \leq y \leq 1} \\[5pt] 0,& \quad \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that \[ \textrm {E}[X]= \dfrac{11}{9},\qquad \textrm {E}[Y]= \dfrac{5}{9}, \qquad \textrm {SD}[X]\approx 0.5329, \qquad \textrm {SD}[Y]\approx 0.2833, \] find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

\[\begin{align} \textrm E [XY] &=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} xy \, f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^2 \left[ \int_0^1 xy \cdot \dfrac{x+y}{3} \: \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3} \int_0^2 \left[ \int_0^1 (x^2y + xy^2) \: \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3} \int_0^2 \left[\dfrac{x^2y^2}{2}+\dfrac{xy^3}{3}\right]_{y=0}^{y=1} \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3} \int_0^2 \left(\dfrac{x^2}2+\dfrac x3\right) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3} \left[ \dfrac{x^3}{6}+\dfrac{x^2}6 \right]_{0}^{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3}. \end{align}\]

Then, we compute the covariance and get

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3} - \left(\dfrac{11}{9}\right)\left(\dfrac{5}{9}\right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{81}. \end{align}

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]} \\[5pt] &\approx \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{1}{81}\right)}{(0.5329) \cdot (0.2833)} \\[5pt] &\approx -0.08, \end{align*}

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

example.title: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Continuous Random Variables

question.text:
\[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{2x+e^{y}}{e}, & \quad {0 \leq x \leq 1, \, 0 \leq y \leq 1} \\[5pt] 0,& \quad \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that \[ \textrm {E}[X]= \dfrac{3e+1}{6e},\qquad \textrm {E}[Y]= \dfrac{3}{2e}, \qquad \textrm {SD}[X]\approx 0.2821, \qquad \textrm {SD}[Y]\approx 0.2870, \] find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

\[\begin{align} \textrm E [XY] &=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} xy \, f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^1 \left[ \int_0^1 xy \cdot \left(\dfrac{2x+e^{y}}{e}\right)\: \textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{e} \int_0^1 \left[ \int_0^1 \left(2x^2y+xye^{y}\right) \: \textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{e} \int_0^1 \left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^3y+\dfrac12x^2ye^{y}\right]_{x=0}^{x=1} \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{e} \int_0^1 \left(\dfrac{2}{3}y+\dfrac12ye^{y}\right) \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{e} \left[ \dfrac{1}{3}y^2+\dfrac12ye^{y}-\dfrac12e^{y}\right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{e} \left(\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{e}{2}-\dfrac{e}{2}+\dfrac 1{2}\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{6e}. \end{align}\]

Then, we compute the covariance and get

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{6e} - \left(\dfrac{3e+1}{6e}\right)\left(\dfrac{3}{2e}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e-3}{12e^2}. \end{align}

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]} \\[5pt] &\approx \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{e-3}{12e^2}\right)}{(0.2821) \cdot (0.2870)} \\[5pt] &\approx -0.04, \end{align*}

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

\[\begin{align} \textrm E [XY] &=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} xy \, f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_{-1}^1 \left[ \int_0^1 xy \cdot\dfrac{xy+2}{4} \: \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4} \int_{-1}^1 \left[ \int_0^1 (x^2y^2 + 2xy) \: \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4} \int_{-1}^1 \left[\dfrac{x^2y^3}{3}+xy^2\right]_{y=0}^{y=1} \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4} \int_{-1}^1 \left(\dfrac{x^2}3+x\right) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4} \left[ \dfrac{x^3}{9}+\dfrac{x^2}2 \right]_{-1}^{1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4} \left[ \dfrac{1}{9}+\dfrac{1}2-\left(-\dfrac{1}{9}+\dfrac{1}2\right) \right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{18}. \end{align}\]

Then, we compute the covariance and get

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{18} - \left(\dfrac{1}{12}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{72}. \end{align}

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]} \\[5pt] &\approx \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{1}{72}\right)}{(0.5713) \cdot (0.2887)} \\[5pt] &\approx 0.08, \end{align*}

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

example.title: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Continuous Random Variables

question.text:
\[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac3{10}(xy^3+2), & \quad {0 \leq 2x \leq y\leq 2} \\[5pt] 0,& \quad \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that \[ \textrm {E}[X]= \dfrac{3}{7},\qquad \textrm {E}[Y]= \dfrac{52}{35}, \qquad \textrm {SD}[X]\approx 0.2575, \qquad \textrm {SD}[Y]\approx 0.4389, \] find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

\[\begin{align} \textrm E [XY] &=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} xy \, f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^1 \left[ \int_{2x}^2 xy \cdot \dfrac3{10}(xy^3+2) \: \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac3{10}\int_0^1 \left[ \int_{2x}^2 \left(x^2y^4+2xy\right)\: \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac3{10}\int_0^1 \left[\dfrac15x^2y^5+xy^2\right]_{y=2x}^{y=2} \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac3{10}\int_0^1 \left(\dfrac{32}5x^2+4x-\dfrac{32}5x^7-4x^3\right) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac3{10}\left[\dfrac{32}{15}x^3+2x^2-\dfrac{4}5x^8-x^4\right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac3{10}\cdot\dfrac{35}{15}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac7{10}. \end{align}\]

Then, we compute the covariance and get

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{7}{10}- \left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)\left(\dfrac{52}{35}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{31}{490}. \end{align}

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]} \\[5pt] &\approx \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{31}{490}\right)}{(0.2575) \cdot (0.4389)} \\[5pt] &\approx 0.56, \end{align*}

rounded to $2$ decimal places.
